extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys, academics, and informed observers of Supreme Court patent jurisprudence
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether software-related patent claims are patent-eligible under the Supreme Court's Alice v. CLS Bank two-part Section 101 framework and related precedents. Focuses on how to determine abstractness and whether an "inventive concept" transforms an abstract idea into a patentable application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-part framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Section 101 framework has two parts: (1) determine if the claim at issue is directed toward an abstract idea; and (2) examine the elements of the claim to determine whether it contains an “inventive concept” sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central test to apply to software patents post-Alice. The article notes the framework was adapted from Mayo and will be the locus of much future argumentation; practitioners should structure analyses around these two steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to-abstract-idea inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the claim covers an abstract idea (e.g., a fundamental economic practice, a mathematical algorithm, or other longstanding conceptual practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recent lodestar cases (Bilski, Alice) as data points: Alice described intermediated settlement as a ‘fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce.' Anti-patterns include claims that are too broad, cover well-known practices, or are drafted comprehensively without meaningful limitations. Examples: Bilski (hedging risk), Alice (intermediated settlement), and cases like Ultramercial likely fail this step post-Alice because of high-level, generalized claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-concept (additional inventive concept) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the elements of the claim to determine whether there is an additional inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This second step asks whether the claimed implementation adds something significantly more than the abstract idea itself. The article observes this can hinge on novel hardware elements or non-conventional uses of technology (see Ancora’s BIOS example). Be aware that courts may treat this similarly to novelty/non-obviousness, creating overlap with other patentability doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth and presence of meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are too broad, that cover well-known practices comprehensively, or that lack meaningful limitations are suspect for being abstract and therefore ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Bilski (claims drawn to the vast bulk of hedging activity) and Alice (claims covering all third-party intermediaries). Draft claims to include concrete, limiting features rather than sweeping functional language to avoid this anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of algorithms and mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms may be assimilated into the category of abstract ideas (following Benson), meaning claims directed to mathematical algorithms risk ineligibility as claims to laws of nature or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns the Court’s assimilation of Benson invites confusion and mischief. Example: PageRank (weighting algorithm) might be characterized as an abstract idea and invalidated if courts view it as claiming ‘weighting’ or a weighting algorithm. Practitioners should consider how to claim application/implementation details that show a practical technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level-of-abstraction in claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The level at which the claim is drafted (highly generalized versus detailed and specific) affects whether a claim is seen as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims drafted at a high level (general steps) are vulnerable — Ultramercial’s view-for-content claims were criticized for generality. Where possible, draft claims to recite concrete, technical steps, limitations, or implementation details to reduce the risk of being categorized as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-conventional / non-generic hardware or specific application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of an abstract idea that employs non-conventional, non-generic hardware or a novel physical implementation may supply the inventive concept needed for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancora (planting encrypted exchange output in BIOS) is cited as an example where using a tricky/hard-to-work-with hardware area could be non-conventional and thus help transform an abstract idea into patentable subject matter. The article suggests that novel hardware elements can matter, but notes many software patents lack such elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with traditional novelty/non-obviousness doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘additional inventive concept’ inquiry can appear duplicative of novelty and non-obviousness requirements, creating tension in its application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be prepared for arguments that conflate Section 101’s inventive-concept requirement with 35 U.S.C. §§ 102/103 analyses. Courts and advocates will debate whether the second step is merely a disguised novelty/non-obviousness test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and uncertainty of applying precedents (interpretive instability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitting earlier Supreme Court cases (e.g., Benson, Bilski, Mayo) into the Alice two-part framework is difficult and creates uncertainty about how abstractness and inventive concept will be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that assimilating older rulings (like Benson) into the new framework invites confusion and may revive discredited reasoning. Expect litigation and divergent lower-court outcomes; arguments should address which precedents to emphasize and how to limit undesirable analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical litigational implications and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alice framework is ‘brief yet baroquely obscure’ and will produce substantial argumentation and case-by-case uncertainty in future litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should anticipate extensive disputes about where a claim falls under the two-step test and prepare multiple lines of argument (e.g., focusing on concrete technical improvements, distinguishing prior cases, or emphasizing non-generic implementations). The article implies strategic claim drafting and litigation posture must account for this unpredictability.
